brief: How to decide what to build next

slots.subline: Six ways teams decide what to build, ranked by how well the decision survives contact with real users.
slots.coverLine: Five of them are ways of avoiding the sixth.

slots.body: The customer who emails four times is one customer who emails four times. Building for them feels responsive and reliably produces a feature nobody else opens, because the people who would have asked simply left instead.
slots.insightText: Count the people who left, not the ones who wrote.

slots.titleMain: Copying puts you a quarter behind, permanently
slots.body: By the time a feature is visible it has already been decided, built and shipped. Matching it means arriving late to a bet somebody else placed on their own customers, not yours.
slots.insightText: Copy the problem they picked, never the answer they shipped.

slots.titleMain: The most senior guess is still a guess
slots.body: Seniority improves the quality of a hypothesis and does nothing at all for its accuracy. The cost is that nobody tests a hypothesis with a title attached to it, so it ships unchecked.
slots.insightText: Write it down as a prediction, then check it in public.

slots.titleMain: Data tells you about the product you already built
slots.body: Every number describes behaviour inside the thing that exists. It is excellent for improving what people do and structurally blind to what they gave up trying, which is where the next product usually is.
slots.insightText: Pair every dashboard with five conversations.

slots.titleMain: The only method that beats the others
slots.body: Sitting with somebody for an hour while they do the job surfaces the workaround they stopped noticing years ago. It scales badly, it cannot be delegated, and it is still the highest-yield hour available.
slots.insightText: Say nothing for the first ten minutes. That is where it is.

slots.titleMain: Deciding well does not make a decision right
slots.body: A good process narrows the range of outcomes; it does not guarantee one. Teams that mistake rigour for certainty stop shipping while they wait to be sure, which is the more expensive failure.
slots.insightText: Optimise for how fast you learn you were wrong.

slots.body: Not a survey, not a dashboard, not a workshop. One person doing the actual job while you keep your mouth shut and write down every workaround.
slots.closingLine: The method that scales worst is the one that works.
slots.signoff: The other five are for arguing with
